why: The Plain translates the Greek. The Hebrew uvlo' ta'mo means "without his sense, his choosing": the husband cannot help sighing. The grandson may have read a different word or guessed.

t: At a cost, or for nothing?
p: Vaticanus says the lender gained an enemy "not for free": it cost him his money. Other copies drop "not": an enemy "for no reason".

why: The Plain follows Swete's text: the lender has lost his money and made an enemy, so the enemy came at a price. Without "not", the line says the lender did nothing to deserve the hatred. Both make sense.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: and for alms you will put him off
readings.plain: and you will keep him waiting for alms

why: Here the Plain departs from Swete's base text. Without "not" the line contradicts its own first half ("be patient with a person in a low position") and the verses that follow (29:9–13). The negative is in Alexandrinus, the Latin and the longer Greek, so its loss in Vaticanus is best explained as a copyist's slip.

a: Be satisfied with a little or a lot.
p: Vaticanus has one line. The longer Greek and the Latin add a second: you will not hear insults as a lodger.

why: The Plain follows Swete's text. The second line, which the KJV and the Latin also have, leads well into 29:24–28, about the insults a lodger must hear; it may have been added to round off the couplet, or lost from Vaticanus.
